claim: Caenorhabditis elegans feeds on bacteria and other small microorganisms which it ingests using its pharynx, a neuromuscular pump.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans feeds on bacteria and other small microorganisms which it ingests using its pharynx, a neuromuscular pump.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans feeding behavior.

claim: Currently, measuring feeding behavior requires tracking a single animal, indirectly estimating food intake from population-level metrics, or using restrained animals.
source: Currently, measuring feeding behavior requires tracking a single animal, indirectly estimating food intake from population-level metrics, or using restrained animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by the comparison table (Table 1) showing existing methods and their limitations.

claim: PharaGlow enables imaging of up to 50 unrestrained crawling worms simultaneously.
source: We image up to 50 unrestrained crawling worms simultaneously and extract locomotion and feeding behaviors.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the methods and results sections of the manuscript.

claim: The C. elegans genome shares at least 50% homology with the human genome.
source: Thanks to its fully sequenced and annotated genome that shares at least 50% homology with human genome and the availability of advanced genome editing tools, short life cycle and transparency, the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans is a powerful model to study feeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claim: C. elegans pumping occurs up to 300 times per minute when food is abundant.
source: On average, pumping occurs up to 300 times per minute when food is abundant (Lee et al., 2017; Song and Avery, 2012; Scholz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pumping is the limiting step for food intake in C. elegans.
source: Pumping is the limiting step for food intake that is, the total food consumed is the product of pumping rate and external food concentration (Seymour et al., 1983; Avery and Shtonda, 2003; Fang-Yen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pumping is inherently a stochastic process.
source: Pumping is inherently a stochastic process (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Even in the absence of food, pumping has been observed and interpreted as a mechanism for food sampling.
source: Even in the absence of food, pumping has been observed and interpreted as a mechanism for food sampling (Lee et al., 2017; Scholz et al., 2017; Trojanowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PharaGlow accurately detects pumping with a deviation of less than 2 pumps per 10 s compared to human expert counting.
source: We found that PharaGlow was able to accurately detect pumping in these videos, and the resulting rate and counts were in agreement with the human expert. Both methods result in a comparable mean pumping rate for the animals counted (Figure 1I), with a deviation between the human and automated results of less than 2 pumps per 10 s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing automated and manual counting shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: The ratio between pharynx and body length decreases from L1 stage to adulthood in C. elegans.
source: During development, the pharynx grows with the body (Knight et al., 2002), but the ratio between pharynx and body length decreases from L1 stage to adulthood (Avery and Shtonda, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: On-food pumping rates increase slightly over the course of larval stages.
source: We find that on-food pumping rates increase slightly over the course of the larval stages, but much less dramatically than the velocity increases over development, despite the substantial growth of both the body and the pharyngeal muscles (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: More than 1000 animal tracks were obtained over the course of three days and five imaging sessions in the developmental study.
source: Over the course of three days and five imaging sessions, more than 1000 animals were tracked, significantly more than can be achieved with comparable methods (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental results.

claim: Pumping rates off food are lower than on food and increase over the course of starvation.
source: Prior work showed that pumping rates off food are lower, but increase over the course of starvation and that this increase is mediated by a cholinergic pathway (You et al., 2006). We track animals either on-, or off food over an increasing amount of starvation time and extract behavioral dynamics (Figure 3A–D). We confirm that pumping is dependent on the starvation duration, with a reduction in pumping rate over the course of three hours (Figure 3B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by both citation to prior work and experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 30 min starvation, a fraction of animals show low speeds and pumping rates, and the remainder are in a high-speed, high pumping state.
source: Taken together, the data suggests that at 30 min starvation, a fraction of the animals show low speeds and pumping rates, and the remainder are in a high-speed, high pumping state (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The decay time of YFP fluorescence signal during continuous imaging is 410±47 min.
source: We find that the decay time of the signal is 410±47 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which indicates that it is possible to do continuous imaging over multiple hours.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: unc-31 mutant animals display reduced, uncoordinated locomotion on food.
source: UNC-31 is involved in dense-core vesicle release, and unc-31 mutant animals display reduced, uncoordinated locomotion on food (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to prior research.

claim: unc-31 animals show long pauses in pumping, unlike wildtype animals.
source: By looking at the individual animals' pumping rates, we find that unc-31 animals show long pauses in pumping, unlike wt animals (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: eat-18 mutant animals were smaller than wildtype.
source: Feeding impaired mutants were previously reported to have reduced body lengths and widths (Mörck and Pilon, 2006). As expected, we found that eat-18 animals were smaller (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citation to prior research.

claim: eat-18 animals developed more slowly, taking approximately 91 hr from egg to adulthood compared to 63 hr for wildtype.
source: As expected, we found that eat-18 animals were smaller (Figure 5C) and developed more slowly (approximately 91 hr from egg to adulthood compared to 63 hr for wildtype).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: eat-18 animals lack the ability to perform fast pumping bursts.
source: We confirmed that eat-18(ad820) animals lack the ability to perform fast pumping bursts (Figure 5B and F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5F.

claim: The duration of a pharyngeal contraction in eat-18 animals is approximately doubled compared to wildtype.
source: the duration of a pharyngeal contraction is approximately doubled compared to wt (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: eat-18 animals showed significantly fewer reversals than wildtype.
source: We also found that eat-18 animals showed significantly fewer reversals than wildtype, indicating a role for the nAch receptor in modulating reversals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: On-food pumping rates are autocorrelated over multi-minute time-scales.
source: These data indicate that on-food pumping rates are autocorrelated over multi-minute time-scales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: unc-31 mutants show more persistent pumping behavior (τ=9.6 min for unc-31(e928) and τ=11.0 min for unc-31(n1304)) compared to wildtype (τ=7.9 min).
source: We therefore tracked animals for at least three hours on food, restrained to our field of view using a copper enclosure. By confining only a few animals (<5 in the field of view), we were able to maintain animal identity over the course of the experiment (see Methods) and quantify their pumping rate over at least 2 hr (Figure 5G). If the population reflects a snapshot of the overall dynamics, a large population measured for a short period of time should result in similar pumping rates as a few animals measured over long time periods. To test this hypothesis, we quantified the autocorrelation of the pumping rate for single worms revealing that pumping rates were correlated for different time scales for wt and unc-31 mutants, with the unc-31 mutants showing a more persistent pumping behavior (τ=9.6 min for unc-31(e928) and τ=11.0 min for unc-31(n1304)) compared to wt (τ=7.9 min) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wild-type animals displayed frequent switching between low and high pumping rates.
source: Wild-type animals displayed frequent switching between low and high pumping rates (Figure 5H and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and 5J.

claim: unc-31 animals displayed infrequent switches between pumping states, consistent with prior reports of constitutive pumping.
source: In contrast, unc-31 animals displayed infrequent switches, consistent with prior reports of constitutive pumping (Avery et al., 1993) and the role of neuropeptides such as PDF in regulating switches between foraging states (Flavell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and 5J and citations to prior research.

claim: The bacteria are ingested and separated from the liquid by the pumping action of the pharyngeal muscles.
source: The bacteria are ingested and separated from the liquid by the pumping action of its powerful pharyngeal muscles (Seymour et al., 1983; Avery and Shtonda, 2003; Fang-Yen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transport of bacteria proceeds with occasional peristaltic contractions that move food toward the terminal bulb where a grinder crushes the bacteria before they are pushed into the intestine.
source: Transport of the bacteria proceeds with occasional peristaltic contractions that move food further toward the terminal bulb where a hard cuticular structure, the grinder, crushes the bacteria before they are pushed into the intestine (Albertson and Thomson, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Stochastic pumping results from a decision making process that serves to regulate pumping based on food availability.
source: It has been suggested that stochastic pumping results from a decision making process that serves to regulate pumping based on food availability (Scholz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and is presented as a suggestion.

claim: Pumping rates are altered in response to the type, concentration, size, and familiarity of the surrounding bacteria.
source: Pumping rates are altered in response to the type, concentration, size, and familiarity of the surrounding bacteria (Lee et al., 2017; Avery and Shtonda, 2003; Scholz et al., 2016; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The behavioral and metabolic context, such as hunger, satiety, and mating drive influence the rate of food intake.
source: The behavioral and metabolic context, such as hunger, satiety, and mating drive also influence the rate of food intake (Avery and Horvitz, 1990; You et al., 2006; You et al., 2008; Gruninger et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Imaging feeding in unrestrained animals is challenging due to the disparate time- and length scales of the motions involved.
source: While desirable, imaging feeding in unrestrained animals, especially in large populations, is challenging due to the disparate time- and length scales of the motions involved. While worms move over centimeters within minutes (Ramot et al., 2008; Swierczek et al., 2011), the observable pharyngeal contractions are over µm within ms (Fang-Yen et al., 2009), making large-scale foraging experiments technically challenging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research describing the scales of motion.

claim: Immobilized animals can introduce artifacts in observed behavior, as the activity of body wall muscles feedbacks to the pharynx via parallel synaptic and hormonal routes.
source: However, these experiments are often performed in immobilized animals, which can introduce artifacts in the observed behavior, as the activity of the body wall muscles feedbacks to the pharynx via parallel synaptic and hormonal routes (Takahashi and Takagi, 2017; Izquierdo et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Using a low magnification of 1x allowed imaging a field of view of 7 by 5 mm.
source: By using a low magnification of 1x, we could image a field of view of 7 by 5 mm, corresponding to multiple body lengths of the worms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental setup shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The pump metric is sensitive to the opening of the pharyngeal lumen and contraction of the terminal bulb.
source: By averaging images during these putative detected pumping events, we determined that this metric is sensitive to the opening of the pharyngeal lumen and contraction of the terminal bulb and thus indeed corresponds to pumping events (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PharaGlow is able to automatically and reliably detect pumping in low-resolution, large field of view images.
source: PharaGlow is therefore able to automatically and reliably detect pumping in low-resolution, large field of view images, enhancing the number of animals which can be scored simultaneously.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with human expert counting shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: The average time from egg to young adult stage for strain GRU101 was 63 hr.
source: The average time from egg to young adult stage for strain GRU101 (gnaIs1[myo-2p::yfp]) was 63 hr.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: The average track duration is well over one minute with 1.9 ± 0.9 min (mean ±s.d.) for L1 and 1.6 ± 0.6 min for adults.
source: The average track duration is well over one minute with 1.9 ± 0.9 min (mean ±s.d.) for L1 and 1.6 ± 0.6 min for adults (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The developmental pumping data represent up to two orders of magnitude more single worm pumping data than is obtainable with conventional methods.
source: These data represent up to two orders of magnitude more single worm pumping data than is obtainable with conventional methods (see Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with methods listed in Table 1.

claim: A small fraction of animals did not show pumping during the recording (5 animal tracks in L1 with <0.5 Hz, <1% for all other conditions).
source: A small fraction of animals did not show pumping during our recording (Figure 2H, 5 animal tracks in L1 with <0.5 Hz, <1% for all other conditions).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In the absence of food, the reversal rate is higher in young adults than in larvae (about 45 events vs 30 events in 10 min), but constant throughout larval development.
source: In the absence of food, the reversal rate is higher in young adults than in larvae (about 45 events vs 30 events in 10 min), but constant throughout larval development (Chiba and Rankin, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Extended exposure to light might affect worm behaviors with a mild light avoidance reaction (5–25%) which depends on the developmental stage.
source: We investigated whether extended exposure to light might affect worm behaviors by monitoring the amount of reversals, pumping rate, and speed. Our results suggest that there is a mild light avoidance reaction (5–25%) which depends on the developmental stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Repeated exposure did not affect behavior in most developmental stages, except for the young adult stage, for which a higher velocity was observed when exposed to light multiple times.
source: Repeated exposure did not affect behavior in most developmental stages, except for the young adult stage, for which a higher velocity was observed when exposed to light multiple times (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Long-term exposure (up to 5 hr) did not affect worm viability.
source: Long-term exposure (up to 5 hr) did not affect worm viability.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Different excitation light did not affect the pumping rate, but had a mild impact on velocity.
source: Lastly, different excitation light did not affect the pumping rate, but had a mild impact on velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 5; see Appendix for details).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Off-food locomotion is faster than on-food locomotion.
source: Off-food locomotion is faster (Dillon et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2005), and pumping irregular (Lee et al., 2017; Scholz et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pumping rates measured immediately after transferring worms off food (<30 min of starvation) were very low in prior studies, possibly due to a lasting pumping suppression after harsh touch.
source: Previously, rates measured immediately after transferring worms off food (<30 min of starvation) were very low, possibly due to a lasting pumping suppression after harsh touch (Keane and Avery, 2003), which we avoid by washing worms off plates instead of picking (see Methods).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison with prior research and the current methodology.

claim: When taken off of food, C. elegans displays a restricted area search (local area search) which is characterized by frequent turns and reversals and an elevated speed.
source: When taken off of food, C. elegans displays a restricted area search (local area search) which is characterized by frequent turns and reversals and an elevated speed (Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Sawin et al., 2000; Calhoun et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The local area search behavior lasts between 30 and 60 min, after which animals switch to longer runs that cover more area.
source: This behavior lasts between 30 and 60 min, after which animals switch to longer runs that cover more area, which is a strategy for dispersal (Hills et al., 2004; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For starved worms at 30 and 90 min, the joint distribution of pumping rates and velocities show distinct sub-populations.
source: Interestingly, for starved worms at 30 and 90 min, the joint distribution of pumping rates and velocities show distinct sub-populations (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: For longer starvation durations, the population becomes homogeneous with a well-defined mean pumping rate and speed.
source: For longer starvation durations, the population becomes homogeneous with a well-defined mean pumping rate and speed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The distinct sub-populations at short starvation times are not apparent in worm populations that stay on food.
source: This is consistent with the fact that these distinct populations are not apparent in worm populations that stay on food (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PharaGlow can track behavior over more than an hour and keep the identity of animals given that these are constrained to the field of view.
source: PharaGlow is therefore able to track behavior over more than an hour, and keep the identity of animals given that these are constrained to the field of view.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mating experiment shown in Figure 4.

claim: It is possible to do continuous imaging over multiple hours without loss of signal.
source: We confirm this observation by calculating photo-bleaching curves. We find that the decay time of the signal is 410±47 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which indicates that it is possible to do continuous imaging over multiple hours.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During a mating attempt, the male shows a larger velocity and performs many long reversals when the animals are close.
source: During the encounter, the male shows a larger velocity and performs many long reversals when the animals are close, as is typical for a mating attempt.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pumping does not completely cease during a mating attempt.
source: It is also interesting to note that pumping does not completely cease during the attempt (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The velocity and pumping distributions differ strongly between the male and hermaphrodite despite being in the same arena.
source: Despite being in the same arena, and covering most of the enclosure during the recording (Figure 4B), the velocity and pumping distributions differ strongly between the two animals (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: unc-31(e928) and unc-31(n1304) animals pump at rates comparable to wildtype.
source: We confirm that unc-31(e928) and unc-31(n1304) animals pump at rates comparable to wildtype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: unc-31 animals show a bimodal distribution of pumping rates with a fraction of animals showing markedly lower rates.
source: However, we see a bimodal distribution of rates with a fraction of animals showing markedly lower rates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EAT-18 is expressed in the pharyngeal muscle and interacts with a nAChR subunit EAT-2 to form a functional acetylcholine receptor.
source: EAT-18 is expressed in the pharyngeal muscle and interacts with a nAChR subunit EAT-2 to form a functional acetylcholine receptor (Raizen et al., 1995; Choudhary et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: eat-18 animals pump at an average rate of 1 Hz.
source: While we detected pumping events at an average rate of 1 Hz, the animals showed a different contraction pattern and timing than either unc-31 or wt animals (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: eat-18 animals were previously reported to rarely pump during experiments (<0.5 Hz).
source: We do observe a higher pumping rate than previously reported for eat-18, where animals were reported to rarely pump during experiments (<0.5 Hz, Raizen et al., 1995; McKay et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: eat-18 animals are able to pump at 1–2 Hz rates.
source: When verifying these sample animals, we did observe slow pumping bursts at the 1–2 Hz rates indicated by PharaGlow, suggesting that these animals are able to pump at this frequency (Figure 5E, arrows and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Video 3.

claim: eat-18 is reported to show expression not only in the pharyngeal muscle, but also in some unidentified somatic neurons.
source: This is likely mediated by extrapharyngeally located neurons, since eat-18 is reported to show expression not only in the pharyngeal muscle, but also in some unidentified somatic neurons (McKay et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Studying the underlying behaviors and dynamics in a worm population requires large statistics and long recordings.
source: Taken together, these results show that studying the underlying behaviors and dynamics in a worm population requires large statistics and long recordings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Uneven plates or improper focus leads to low signal-to-noise ratios.
source: We find that uneven plates or improper focus leads to low signal-to-noise ratios.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Small variations of the worm height do not affect the result, as low-magnification imaging results in a large depth of field.
source: Additionally, once at focus, small variations of the worm height do not affect the result, as low-magnification imaging results in a large depth of field.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of optical principles and experimental observations.

claim: The data rate of the large area scan cameras is >6 GB/min.
source: On a 4-core laptop, the expected analysis time is approximately 8 hr for 150 worm-minutes of data. While the analysis can be run on a laptop or desktop computer, runtime is much improved when using a computing cluster (see Supplementary materials).
evidence: This is a direct report of the data handling requirements.

claim: On a 4-core laptop, the expected analysis time is approximately 8 hr for 150 worm-minutes of data.
source: On a 4-core laptop, the expected analysis time is approximately 8 hr for 150 worm-minutes of data.
evidence: This is a direct report of the computational requirements.

claim: The method provides an increase in throughput by more than one order of magnitude compared to manual methods.
source: Our fully automatic method provides an increase in throughput by more than one order of magnitude, and does not require any laborious handling of the animals or microfluidic devices.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with manual counting methods.

claim: The imaging does not adversely affect worms, allowing animals to be imaged multiple times.
source: As our imaging does not adversely affect worms, animals can be imaged multiple times, as we demonstrated by following pumping in a population of developing animals or can be imaged continuously for hours as shown for the mating animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the developmental and mating experiments.

claim: The method creates opportunities for studying novel behaviors, such as foraging in complex environments or behavioral coordination.
source: In addition, by enabling measurements of unrestrained animals directly on agarose plates, our approach creates opportunities for studying novel behaviors, such as foraging in complex environments (Ding et al., 2020; Iwanir et al., 2016) or behavioral coordination (Cermak et al., 2020; Hardaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the capabilities of the method.

claim: Resolving the decisions underlying feeding behavior requires temporal resolution to correlate pumping with neural activity.
source: To understand the neural basis of feeding, resolving the decisions underlying feeding behavior is required (Scholz et al., 2017; Katzen et al., 1983). However, current bulk methods capable of extracting population averages of pumping rates are insufficient to understand underlying neural activity, as the data lack the temporal resolution to correlate pumping with neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for understanding neural mechanisms.

claim: The method enables the quantification of pumping activity, in multiple animals simultaneously, as a marker of feeding behavior in C. elegans.
source: Our method enables the quantification of pumping activity, in multiple animals simultaneously, as a marker of feeding behavior in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the method's capabilities.

claim: Observed feeding defects likely differ between crawling, food-stimulated animals and serotonin-stimulated animals.
source: Immobilization often requires the addition of serotonin (5-HT) to stimulate pumping, as pumping is suppressed in restrained animals (Takahashi and Takagi, 2017). It is likely that observed feeding defects differ between crawling, food-stimulated animals and serotonin-stimulated animals (Lee et al., 2017), and that new experiments will be effective in identifying phenotypes that went unnoticed in immobilized preparations.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known differences between experimental conditions.

claim: Testing models of patch foraging while explicitly including measured food intake will help better define the limits in which simple models of foraging are applicable.
source: Testing models of patch foraging and their predictions (Davidson and El Hady, 2019) while explicitly including measured food intake will help better define the limits in which simple models of foraging are applicable.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: The myo-2 gene is a myosin heavy chain that is conserved among nematodes and will likely show similar expression in closely related species.
source: While the requirement for labeling the muscle is a prerequisite of our method, the myo-2 gene is a myosin heavy chain that is conserved among nematodes and will likely show similar expression in closely related species.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene conservation and a speculation about applicability to other species.

claim: A strain with the myo-2 promoter construct for the closely related C. briggsae is already available at the CGC.
source: A strain with the myo-2 promoter construct for the closely related C. briggsae is already available at the CGC.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about available resources.

claim: The power density of fluorescence excitation at the focal plane was 0.24 mW/mm2 at 500 nm.
source: The power density of fluorescence excitation at the focal plane (0.24 mW/mm2 at 500 nm) was measured using a power meter sensor (PS19Q; Coherent) with the corresponding controller (PowerMax; Coherent).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Animals were imaged at 30 fps for 5 min unless otherwise indicated.
source: Animals were imaged at 30 fps for 5 min unless otherwise indicated.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental protocol.

claim: For long-term imaging, stroboscopic illumination (5ms light pulses) were used to reduce bleaching.
source: For long-term imaging, stroboscopic illumination (5ms light pulses) were used to reduce bleaching.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental protocol.

claim: The live segmentation method allowed storing only areas containing worms and their coordinates, resulting in a data reduction by approximately 1000 fold.
source: To reduce the amount of stored data and allow continuous recording using a standard computer (Celsius W520; Fujitsu), images were segmented automatically and only areas containing worms, and their coordinates within the image, were stored. This procedure allowed a data reduction by approximately 1000 fold.
evidence: This is a direct report of the data handling method and its efficiency.

claim: The magnification for each developmental stage was chosen to achieve an approximate pharynx length of ~60 pixels.
source: The magnification for each stage was chosen to achieve an approximate pharynx length of ~60 pixels (2 x (1.18 µm/px) for L1, 1.5 x (1.57 µm/px) for L2, 1.4 x (1.69 µm/px) for L3, 1.3 x (1.81 µm/px) for L4 and the standard 1 x (2.36 µm/px) for young adults).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental protocol.

claim: PharaGlow runs a three-step analysis: center of mass tracking and collision detection, linking detected objects to trajectories, and extracting centerline, contour, width, and other parameters of the shape to allow extracting pharyngeal pumping events.
source: In brief, PharaGlow runs a three-step analysis: 1. center of mass tracking and collision detection, 2. linking detected objects to trajectories and 3. extracting centerline, contour, width, and other parameters of the shape to allow extracting pharyngeal pumping events.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis pipeline.

claim: The code is fully modular and any existing tracking code could in principle be used for the first two steps provided the input data is formatted to PharaGlow standards.
source: The code is fully modular and any existing tracking code could in principle be used for the first two steps provided the input data is formatted to PharaGlow standards.
evidence: This is a description of the software design.

claim: Peaks in the pumping metric trace correspond to pumping events.
source: This metric is sensitive to the opening of the pharyngeal lumen and terminal bulb contractions. Peaks in the resulting trace correspond to pumping events.
evidence: This is based on the analysis method and validation shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A rolling mean filter of 1 s is used to correct for baseline fluctuations and spurious fluorescence changes (except for eat-18 mutants, where 3 s is used).
source: We correct for baseline fluctuations and spurious fluorescence changes by subtracting the background fluctuations using a rolling mean filter of 1 s (except for eat-18 mutants, where we use 3 s otherwise the slow contractions were removed too).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: AMPD algorithm is used for peak detection in quasi-periodic signals.
source: We detect peaks using AMPD, an algorithm for peak detection in quasi-periodic signals (Scholkmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citation to the algorithm.

claim: Velocity was calculated from the tracked center of mass of the labeled pharynx.
source: Velocity was calculated from the tracked center of mass of the labeled pharynx.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: Reversals were calculated based on the angle between the pharynx and the animal's nose tip direction.
source: Reversals were calculated based on the angle between the pharynx and the animal's nose tip direction.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: Timepoints with angles exceeding 120° were annotated as reversals.
source: Timepoints with angles exceeding 120° were annotated as reversals.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: All animals that were successfully tracked for at least 60 s were included in the analysis for Figures 1-3.
source: All animals that were successfully tracked for at least 60 s (Figures 1—3) were included. No other filtering or outlier removal was performed.
evidence: This is a description of the data inclusion criteria.

claim: For eat-18 mutants, only animals that had the appropriate size for their stage were included.
source: For eat-18 mutants, the size and developmental stage of the animals were more dispersed and only animals that had the appropriate size for their stage were included (Figure 5).
